lines.text: A test tells you a change is right.
It does not tell you how the cost will grow when the data does.
For that you need a small vocabulary, big O, big omega and big theta, and logarithms in any base.
This is the last of the five refreshers. If it is all familiar, swipe on to the memory hierarchy.
Think of big O as a ceiling. From some size on, the cost stays under a fixed multiple of a simple function.
Omega is the floor. Theta is both at once, a ceiling and a floor of the same shape.
Now watch the job on screen. It takes a few n log n steps plus a few n. Divide by n log n and look at what is left: from a certain size on, the ratio sits in a narrow band.
That is the proof of theta of n log n. The constant multiplier and the extra n do not change the shape, so they drop out.
You have just shown the job is theta of n log n. A reviewer writes, in a comment, that it is big O of n squared.
Before you answer, remember what big O promises: only a ceiling.
Is the comment true?
Yes, it is true, and it is nearly useless.
A logarithm is never bigger than n, so n squared is a ceiling on this job, just a very loose one, more than a million times too high at a hundred million rows.
So big O alone never says slow. And it is not a case either: the best case and the worst case of any algorithm can each have an O, an omega and a theta. Say theta when you mean the growth rate.
Let the data grow and watch the bars. They are on a log scale, so each gridline is a factor of ten.
At a thousand rows, everything is instant and nothing matters. At a hundred million orders, a linear job takes a tenth of a second, and n log n under three.
Now look at the tallest bar. Quadratic work takes months.
Double the data and the linear job doubles, n log n grows slightly more, and n squared quadruples. That is the intuition to carry.

lines.text: Now logarithms. A logarithm counts divisions: how many times can you divide by the base before you reach one?
You have seen the number already. Bisecting a thousand commits took about ten tests, because a thousand halves down to one in about ten steps.
Use that to estimate a bigger one. Each ten halvings divide by about a thousand.
How many times do you halve a billion to reach one?

tolerated.line: How many times do you halve a billion to reach one?

lines.text: About thirty.
A billion is a thousand times a thousand times a thousand, so it takes ten halvings three times.
Every thousand times more data costs only ten more halvings.
So a million times more data is only twenty more steps.
That is the whole appeal of a logarithm.

tolerated.line: A billion is a thousand times a thousand times a thousand, so it takes ten halvings three times.

lines.text: You will see logs in many bases, so one formula is enough. Divide the natural log of the number by the natural log of the base.
On screen, one length measured with three rulers: base two, base ten, and base a thousand. The length does not change, only the unit.
A mental shortcut: log base two is about three point three times log base ten. A billion has nine zeros, so about thirty halvings.
Now notice what the base does. The bigger the base, the fewer the divisions.
A billion needs thirty halvings, but only three divisions by a thousand, and just over two by sixteen thousand.
Indexes and sorts divide by hundreds or thousands at a time, not by two. So their logarithms are tiny, and that is why a database can find a row among a billion in a handful of steps.
Use it on a real structure. A hundred million orders, with a B-tree index on the order id.
A page holds about four hundred entries, and each inner entry points to a page below. So each level multiplies the reach by about four hundred.
Root to leaf.
How many levels?
Four.
Three levels reach only about sixty four million keys, short of a hundred million. The fourth takes the reach past twenty five billion.
The answer is robust: any fan out from a hundred to over four hundred and sixty gives four levels. A binary tree over the same keys would need twenty seven.
Sorting is the same logarithm, with an enormous base. Follow the passes on screen.
The nightly job sorts about a trillion bytes with memory for sixteen thousand blocks. The first pass makes sixty four sorted runs.
The merge can take sixteen thousand runs at once, so one more pass merges all sixty four. Two passes in total, each reading and writing everything.
Merge two at a time instead, and it is seven passes. The base of the logarithm is the memory.
A warning, because big O is often misread as a stopwatch. It throws away constants on purpose, to compare growth on any hardware.
So it cannot give you seconds. Look at the two scans of the same hundred million rows: the same count, the same growth, completely different times.
The difference is where each step finds its data. In a cache, a tenth of a second. Waiting on a disk, hours.
Keep that in mind. It is the reason the next topic exists.
Five things to keep. Big O is a ceiling, omega a floor, theta both.
A logarithm counts divisions, and any base converts with a natural log. A big base makes a tiny logarithm: four levels, two passes.
And big O counts steps, not seconds.
Next up: the memory hierarchy, where one step can cost a nanosecond or tens of milliseconds.
